result: Platynereis nectochaete larvae possess segmentally arranged ciliated fields including the prototroch (23 cells), akrotroch (8 cells), nuchal cilia (6 cells), crescent cell (1 cell), metatroch (8 cells), and three paratroch bands (8, 14, and 12 cells respectively). These anatomical features were characterized using scanning electron microscopy and serial TEM reconstruction.
evaluation: Claims C1-C7 and C21-C24 provide comprehensive anatomical characterization of ciliated structures supported by multiple imaging modalities (SEM, TEM, connectome reconstruction). The cell counts and spatial organization are consistently documented across techniques, providing strong convergent evidence for the anatomical organization.

result: Ciliary arrests occur synchronously across all ciliary bands in Platynereis larvae, with cilia resuming beating first in the prototroch followed by paratroch cilia with a 19±3 msec delay. These arrests correlate with periodic synchronous increases in calcium signals in ciliary band cells.
evaluation: Claims C8-C10 and C12 demonstrate coordinated ciliary behavior through DIC imaging and calcium imaging with GCaMP6s. The quantitative timing measurements and correlation with calcium dynamics provide strong evidence for synchronized whole-body ciliary coordination.

result: The crescent cell exhibits distinct ciliary behavior compared to locomotor cilia, with cilia beating when other cilia are arrested despite showing simultaneous calcium increases. Crescent cilia have lower density, beat irregularly, and lack metachronal wave organization.
evaluation: Claims C13-C16 document the unique properties of crescent cell cilia through imaging data showing anti-phase beating patterns and structural differences. The observation of simultaneous calcium signals but opposite behavioral responses indicates distinct regulatory mechanisms.

result: Ciliary activity correlates with the time derivative of calcium (d[Ca2+]i/dt) rather than absolute calcium concentration, with cilia arrested during calcium increases and resuming beating when calcium levels drop.
evaluation: Claims C17-C19 are supported by high frame rate calcium imaging analysis showing correlation between ciliary state and calcium dynamics. This represents a mechanistic insight into how calcium signals control ciliary behavior, analogous to findings in sea urchin sperm (C20).

result: The MC neuron is a large biaxonal cholinergic neuron with soma in the larval head center that projects bilaterally to innervate all 23 prototroch cells. It is the most synapse-rich neuron in the connectome with 341 presynaptic sites, 335 targeting prototroch cells.
evaluation: Claims C25-C33 provide detailed anatomical characterization of the MC neuron through connectome reconstruction, showing its unique morphology and comprehensive innervation pattern. The quantitative synapse counts and complete connectivity to all prototroch cells are well-documented.

result: Loop neurons are large biaxonal cholinergic neurons with somas in the first trunk segment that project axons forming complete loops around the larval body. Each Loop neuron synapses on every ipsilateral paratroch cell, akrotroch, nuchal cilia, lateral prototroch cells, and the crescent cell, innervating all locomotor ciliary fields except the metatroch.
evaluation: Claims C34-C43 describe the remarkable morphology and connectivity of Loop neurons through connectome reconstruction. The documentation of complete body-spanning projections and comprehensive ipsilateral innervation patterns is well-supported by anatomical data.

result: Six ventral cholinergic motorneurons (vMNs) form three left-right pairs with distinct projection patterns: MNr1/MNl1 innervate ventral structures, MNr2/MNl2 innervate lateral and dorsal structures, and MNr3/MNl3 are purely ciliomotor neurons targeting lateral prototroch cells. The eyespotPRCR3 photoreceptors directly synapse on prototroch cells.
evaluation: Claims C44-C49 characterize the ventral motorneuron system through connectome reconstruction, showing distinct connectivity patterns for different neuron pairs. The identification of purely ciliomotor versus dual ciliary-muscle innervating neurons is well-documented.

result: The cholinergic identity of ciliomotor neurons is supported by pharmacological experiments, expression of cholinergic markers (ChAT, VAChT), and transgenic labeling with sGCβ1 reporter. Loop and MNl3 neurons were confirmed cholinergic through transgenic labeling, while MC neuron identity is supported by VAChT expression and pharmacology.
evaluation: Claims C50-C56 provide multiple lines of evidence for cholinergic identity including molecular markers, transgenic reporters, and pharmacology. The convergence of different methods strengthens the neurotransmitter assignments, though single-cell resolution confirmation is lacking for some neurons (MNant cells).

result: Five serotonergic ciliomotor neurons were identified: two head neurons (Ser-h1) that cross the midline to innervate contralateral prototroch, and two trunk neurons (Ser-tr1) that are among the largest neurons in the connectome (1,600-1,850 µm cable length) and innervate all paratroch cells and metatroch. Ser-tr1 axons run parallel to Loop neurons but are ultrastructurally distinct.
evaluation: Claims C57-C69 characterize serotonergic neurons through connectome reconstruction, immunostaining, and transgenic labeling. The identification is well-supported by multiple methods including TrpH reporter expression and serotonin antibody staining, with detailed morphological and connectivity data.

result: A giant serotonergic sensory-motor neuron (pygPBbicil) with cell body in the pygidium has two sensory cilia and two axons that project anteriorly to innervate prototroch cilia. This neuron expresses both serotonin and FMRFamide and represents the third sensory neuron that directly synapses on ciliated cells.
evaluation: Claims C70-C75 describe a unique sensory-motor neuron identified through connectome reconstruction, immunostaining, and siGOLD labeling. The dual sensory-motor nature and co-expression of serotonin and neuropeptide are well-documented.

result: Three molecularly distinct peptidergic neurons (cMNvl, cMNd, cMNATO) with cell bodies at the prototroch level express different combinations of neurotransmitters and neuropeptides. cMNvl and cMNATO express tyrosine hydroxylase (dopaminergic), cMNATO also expresses dopamine-β-hydroxylase (noradrenergic), and all express various neuropeptides (PDF, allatotropin, FLamide, FVamide, DLamide, L11, LYamide). These neurons synapse on prototroch cells, the MC cell, and reciprocally among themselves.
evaluation: Claims C76-C84 provide comprehensive molecular characterization through in situ hybridization, immunostaining, and siGOLD labeling. The complex neurotransmitter/neuropeptide profiles and connectivity patterns are well-documented, though the functional implications of this molecular diversity require further investigation.

result: Network modularity analysis subdivides the ciliomotor system into three communities: Module 1 contains neurons innervating only prototroch cells, Module 2 contains neurons innervating primarily right-side ciliated cells, and Module 3 contains neurons innervating primarily left-side ciliated cells.
evaluation: Claims C85-C88 apply computational network analysis to connectome data to identify functional modules. The modularity analysis is appropriately applied and reveals organizational principles, though the biological significance of this particular modular organization could be more thoroughly validated.

result: Extensive interconnections exist between ciliomotor neurons of different neurotransmitter types: cMN neurons are presynaptic to MC, MNant, and Loop neurons and reciprocally connected with Ser-h1 and pygPBbicil cells; Ser-h1 cells are presynaptic to MC; Ser-tr1 and Loop neurons are reciprocally connected; and pygPBbicil is presynaptic to MC.
evaluation: Claims C89-C93 document inter-neuronal connectivity patterns from connectome reconstruction. These connections suggest complex circuit interactions between different neurotransmitter systems, providing anatomical substrate for coordinated activity.

result: cMN neurons display spontaneous rhythmic activity patterns detectable from 24 hpf onwards, with cMNvl and cMNd showing rhythmic increases in GCaMP signal synchronous with ciliary bands, while cMNATO activity is negatively correlated with the other cMN neurons and ciliary band.
evaluation: Claims C94-C97 demonstrate rhythmic neuronal activity through calcium imaging. The opposing activity patterns of cMNATO versus cMNvl/cMNd suggest these neurons may play antagonistic roles in rhythm generation, consistent with their distinct molecular profiles.

result: The MC neuron exhibits periodic activity strongly correlated with prototroch cell activity and ciliary arrests, with a median cycle length of 71 seconds (43% of larvae showing 50-100 s cycles). Loop neurons in the trunk also activate synchronously with ciliary band cells.
evaluation: Claims C98-C102 characterize MC and Loop neuron activity through calcium imaging in multiple larvae (n=96). The quantitative analysis of cycle length and correlation with ciliary arrests provides strong evidence for the role of these neurons in coordinating ciliary behavior.

result: Laser ablation of the MC neuron eliminates rhythmic activity in prototroch cells and most ciliary arrests, demonstrating that the MC cell is essential for triggering rhythmic arrests of prototroch cilia.
evaluation: Claims C103-C104 provide causal evidence for MC neuron function through targeted ablation experiments. The loss of rhythmic arrests following ablation directly demonstrates necessity, though the inference of sufficiency would require additional experiments.

result: Alpha-bungarotoxin treatment decouples MC neuron activity from ciliary band activity, with the MC neuron continuing rhythmic activation while calcium signals disappear in ciliary bands and arrests are eliminated. This indicates cholinergic signaling is required for ciliary arrests but not for neuronal rhythm generation.
evaluation: Claims C105-C107 use pharmacological manipulation to dissect the role of cholinergic transmission. The continued MC neuron activity despite loss of ciliary responses provides strong evidence that the rhythm is generated upstream of cholinergic transmission to cilia.

result: Three ventral MN cells show either synchronous or asynchronous activity with ciliary bands. Following MC neuron ablation, prototroch activity correlates with vMNsync neuron activity, suggesting this cholinergic neuron can maintain a lower rate of prototroch activation.
evaluation: Claims C108-C110 characterize ventral MN activity and their relationship to ciliary activity. The post-ablation correlation suggests compensatory mechanisms, though the functional significance and identity of specific vMN cells could be more definitively established.

result: Head serotonergic cells (Ser-h1) and trunk serotonergic cells (Ser-tr1) show anti-correlated activity with ciliated cells and MC neuron. The identity of Ser-tr1 neurons was confirmed through photoactivation experiments followed by serotonin immunostaining (n=11 larvae).
evaluation: Claims C111-C113 demonstrate anti-phase activity of serotonergic neurons through calcium imaging and confirm cell identity through innovative photoactivation-immunostaining approach. The anti-correlation suggests serotonergic neurons are active during ciliary beating phases.

result: Exogenous serotonin application increases ciliary beat frequency and inhibits ciliary arrests compared to untreated larvae.
evaluation: Claims C114-C115 demonstrate pharmacological effects of serotonin on ciliary behavior. The results are consistent with the anti-correlated activity of serotonergic neurons, though the site of action (direct on cilia vs. on circuit) remains unclear.

result: The ciliomotor system constitutes a stop-and-go pacemaker circuit where synchronous rhythmic activation of cholinergic cells drives coordinated ciliary arrests, serotonergic cells are active during ciliary beating and inhibit the cholinergic rhythm while increasing beat frequency, and catecholaminergic cells may generate the rhythm based on their connectivity and alternating activity.
evaluation: Claims C116, C148-C152 synthesize the functional organization of the ciliomotor circuit based on connectivity, activity patterns, ablation, and pharmacology. The stop-and-go model is well-supported by converging evidence, though the role of catecholaminergic cells in rhythm generation (C152) remains inferential and requires direct testing.

result: The rhythm is generated by interactions of ciliomotor neurons themselves, supported by reciprocal synaptic connections between neurons. The cMN neurons are candidate rhythm generators as they show the earliest rhythmic activity during development, contain cells with distinct transmitter profiles suggesting antagonistic signaling, are presynaptic to all other ciliomotor neurons, and coordinate MC and Loop neuron activity. Cholinergic neurons are excluded from rhythm generation as blocking cholinergic transmission does not eliminate MC neuron rhythmic activation.
evaluation: Claims C153-C159 propose a mechanism for rhythm generation based on connectivity patterns, developmental timing, molecular profiles, and pharmacology. The evidence is strong but indirect; definitive identification of the pacemaker neurons would require targeted manipulations of cMN neurons.

result: The MC neuron together with two Loop neurons triggers coordinated body-wide ciliary arrests by innervating all multiciliated cells except the metatroch. Metatroch arrests may be triggered by MNant neurons, the only putatively cholinergic neurons innervating the metatroch.
evaluation: Claims C160-C162 integrate connectivity and functional data to propose the effector mechanism for ciliary arrests. The inference is well-supported by the comprehensive innervation pattern and MC ablation results, though the role of Loop neurons and MNant neurons in metatroch control remains to be directly tested.

result: The crescent cell receives synaptic input exclusively from Loop neurons but responds oppositely to locomotor cilia, starting to beat instead of arresting. The beating of crescent cilia may serve to generate water flow for chemosensory sampling in the apical organ.
evaluation: Claims C165-C166 document unique connectivity and behavior of the crescent cell, but C167's proposed function is speculative. While the analogy to olfactory flow generation in fish is reasonable, direct evidence for chemosensory function is lacking. The mechanism underlying opposite responses to the same input also requires investigation.

result: Four serotonergic ciliomotor neurons collectively innervate all ciliary bands and are presynaptic to cholinergic cells. Serotonin application suppresses closures and increases beat frequency. Serotonergic cell activation corresponds to swimming periods, suggesting they are responsible for resumption of beating, potentially acting through pacemaker modulation or directly on ciliated cells.
evaluation: Claims C168-C170 and C173-C174 are well-supported by connectivity and activity data, but C171-C172 regarding mechanism of action are speculative. The correlation between serotonergic activity and swimming is strong, but distinguishing between direct effects on cilia versus circuit modulation requires additional experiments.

result: Loop and Ser-tr1 neurons span twice the entire body length to coordinately regulate segmental cilia, and many ciliomotor neurons have biaxonal morphology, a feature rare in other Platynereis circuits.
evaluation: Claims C117-C118 and C182 highlight unique morphological features of ciliomotor neurons supported by connectome reconstruction and comparison to other circuits. The body-spanning morphology is remarkable and well-documented, providing anatomical basis for whole-body coordination.

result: Serotonergic, catecholaminergic, and cholinergic innervation of ciliary bands has been described across multiple animal groups including annelids, molluscs, phoronids, bryozoans, echinoderms, hemichordates, and nemerteans, suggesting these ciliomotor systems may be ancestral features. Comparative studies suggest similar systems with large biaxonal neurons are widespread in ciliated larvae.
evaluation: Claims C119-C122 and C183 are supported by citations to comparative morphological literature. However, the inference of homology versus convergent evolution cannot be definitively determined from the cited histological studies alone. The comparative data support conservation of neurotransmitter types but not necessarily circuit organization.

result: One scenario is that ciliated larvae and their nervous systems, including ciliomotor systems, are homologous across bilaterians or eumetazoans, suggesting the Platynereis ciliomotor system may represent an ancient system that evolved close to the origin of nervous systems, with internal coordination of multiciliated surfaces being an early nervous system function.
evaluation: Claims C123-C125 present speculative evolutionary hypotheses explicitly acknowledged as controversial. While the comparative data on neurotransmitter types provide some support, the claims about deep homology of entire larval nervous systems require much more extensive comparative connectomic and developmental data to evaluate properly.

result: The alternation of swimming and sinking periods maintains larval depth in the water column. The larval nervous system exhibits rhythmic autonomic activity from the 1-day-old stage with <20 neurons, present in all larvae without sensory input induction. This ongoing activity can be modulated by neuromodulators (neuropeptides, melatonin) and sensory input through neuroendocrine signaling.
evaluation: Claims C176-C181 integrate behavioral, developmental, and neuromodulatory data supported by citations and calcium imaging. The characterization of early autonomous rhythmic activity and its modulation provides important context for understanding the biological function and regulation of the ciliomotor system.
